title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
section: Limitation 1: The Equivalent Couple Problem (Spatial Ambiguity)
text:
Limitation 1: The Equivalent Couple Problem (Spatial Ambiguity)

Force-Couple Equivalence in Rigid Body Mechanics
definition: [Force-Couple Equivalence] Any system of forces acting on a rigid body can be reduced to a statically equivalent system consisting of: - A single resultant force \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{eq}}\) acting at an arbitrary reference point

A couple \(\mathbf{C}_{\text{eq}}\) (pure moment) This equivalence is dynamic: both systems produce identical translational and rotational accelerations of the rigid body.

The fundamental principle is that a couple is a free vector—it can act anywhere on the rigid body without changing the body’s motion. In contrast, a force is bound to its line of action; relocating the point of application requires introducing or modifying a couple to maintain dynamic equivalence.
[Figure: Force-couple equivalence: a force \(\mathbf{F}\)]


Coordinate Transformation of Force-Couple Pairs
For a rigid body such as a golf club, if inverse dynamics yields force \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{eq}}\) and couple \(\mathbf{C}_{\text{eq}}\) at reference point \(m\), we can transform these to an equivalent force-couple pair at any other point \(i\) along the grip.
This transformation reveals a crucial insight: the equivalent couple is not an intrinsic property of the force distribution but depends on the choice of reference point.
[Figure: Golf club grip schematic showing reference points and distance measures. The center of mass (COM) is closer to the clubhead than to the hands. Distances are measured with consistent sign convention.]


The Range of Equivalent Couples
From Equation~[@eq:couple_transform], we can determine the range of equivalent couples for a given inverse dynamics result as the reference point varies along the grip.
At the top of the grip:
\[
C_t = M_m \left(1 - \frac{d_t}{d_m}\right) + C_m
\]
At the bottom of the grip:
\[
C_b = M_m \left(1 - \frac{d_b}{d_m}\right) + C_m
\]

Key Point: The range of viable equivalent couples increases linearly with the moment of force \(M_m = F \cdot d_m\). For larger forces or forces acting farther from the center of mass, the spatial ambiguity grows substantially.

[Figure: Equivalent couple as a function of position along the grip for three different moments of force, with constant \(C_m = -4.0\) Nm at the midpoint. The region between dashed lines represents typical hand placement. Note how the range of possible couple values increases with \(M_m\).]


Physical Interpretation: The Non-Uniqueness Problem
The mathematical transformation in Equation~[@eq:couple_transform] has a profound physical consequence: a couple appearing in inverse dynamics results does not necessarily correspond to any actual twisting action by the golfer.
This example reveals the core issue: inverse dynamics conflates two physically distinct phenomena: 1. True couples: Opposing forces applied simultaneously (e.g., left hand pulls up while right hand pushes down)

Offset forces: Single or net forces applied away from the reference point

[Figure: Two physically distinct force applications that produce identical inverse dynamics results at the reference point. Left: True couple from opposing forces. Right: Apparent couple from single offset force. Inverse dynamics cannot distinguish between them.]


Implications for Distributed Force Application
In reality, golfers apply forces at multiple points on the grip: individual fingers, palm heel, thumb pads, etc. Each force contributes to both the net force and the equivalent couple at any chosen reference point.
[Figure: Inverse dynamics reduces distributed forces from multiple fingers and palm contact points to a single equivalent force and couple at the reference point. This reduction is mathematically valid but loses information about the spatial distribution.]

Fundamental Limitation: Without knowledge of where forces are applied along the grip, inverse dynamics results are fundamentally ambiguous. The same force-couple pair could arise from: - Strong forces applied close to the reference point

Weaker forces applied far from the reference point
Any combination with the same resultant and moment

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
text:
Limitation 2: The Control-Affine Decomposition Problem

Control-Affine Systems: A Framework for Understanding Motion
The spatial ambiguity discussed in Section 2 is compounded by a deeper challenge rooted in the structure of the system dynamics. The golf club-golfer system is naturally described as a control-affine system.
definition: [Control-Affine System] A control-affine system is a dynamical system of the form:
\[
{#eq-control_affine}
\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}
\]
where: - \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the state vector (positions and velocities)

\(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\) is the drift vector field (system dynamics without input)
\(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})\) is the input matrix (how controls affect the state)
\(\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) is the control input vector

The key feature is the additive separation of drift and input effects. This decomposition reflects a fundamental physical distinction:

Drift (\(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\)): Passive dynamics arising from the system’s configuration, including gravitational forces, inertial effects (centrifugal, Coriolis), and constraint forces in closed kinematic chains
Input (\(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}\)): Active control—forces that the controller (golfer) can directly modulate. This is what the golfer feels and what they exert effort toward achieving.


Key Point: The input component represents what the golfer consciously controls and experiences as effort. When a golfer “feels” like they are pulling or pushing, they are sensing the input forces they must actively generate, not the total forces (which include passive dynamics).



Inverse Dynamics in the Lagrangian Framework
To understand what inverse dynamics calculates, we examine the Lagrangian formulation. For a system with generalized coordinates \(\mathbf{q}\), the equations of motion are:
\[
{#eq-lagrange}
\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}
\]
where: - \(\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\) is the mass/inertia matrix

\(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\) contains Coriolis and centrifugal terms
\(\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q})\) contains gravitational and other conservative force terms
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) are the generalized forces (what we want to find)

Inverse dynamics solves for \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) given observed \(\mathbf{q}(t)\), \(\dot{\mathbf{q}}(t)\), and \(\ddot{\mathbf{q}}(t)\):
\[
{#eq-inverse_dynamics}
\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{q})
\]


The Fundamental Problem: Inseparability of Drift and Input
Here is the critical observation: inverse dynamics computes the total generalized force \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), which includes both drift and input components:
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{total}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{drift}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{input}}
\]
In the control-affine formulation, these correspond to:
\[
\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{drift}} &= \text{generalized forces from } \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) \\
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{input}} &= \text{generalized forces from } \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}
\end{align}
\]

Fundamental Limitation: Inverse dynamics cannot distinguish between these components without additional information. The calculation yields \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{total}}\), but this single measurement corresponds to infinitely many possible \((drift, input)\) pairs satisfying:
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{drift}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{input}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{total}}
\]

[Figure: Forward vs. inverse dynamics in control-affine systems. Forward: drift and input combine uniquely to produce motion. Inverse: given motion alone, we cannot uniquely recover the drift-input decomposition.]


Why a Model is Necessary
To separate drift from input, we need an explicit model of the system. Specifically:

Kinematic model: How the system’s generalized coordinates relate to physical positions and orientations
Dynamic model: The equations of motion including:

Mass and inertia properties



Gravitational effects
Constraint forces (for closed chains)
Velocity-dependent terms (centrifugal, Coriolis)


Control model: Which degrees of freedom are directly actuated and which forces are controllable

With such a model, we can: 1. Calculate \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{drift}}\) from the observed state \((\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\) using the drift dynamics

Obtain \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{input}}\) by subtraction: \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{input}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{total}} - \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{drift}}\)


Key Point: The necessity of a model for interpreting inverse dynamics is often underappreciated. Without a model specifying how passive and active forces contribute to motion, we cannot determine “what the golfer is doing” from motion data alone—we only know “what is happening to the club.”



Relevance to Golf Biomechanics
In the golf swing, significant forces arise from passive dynamics:

Gravitational forces: The club weighs approximately 0.5-1 lb, creating torques about pivot points
Centrifugal forces: The rotating club creates substantial outward forces that the golfer must counteract or utilize
Coriolis forces: Changes in angular velocity create velocity-dependent forces
Kinematic constraint forces: In a double-pendulum model (common for golf swing analysis), constraint forces arise from the requirement that body segments remain connected

When inverse dynamics reports, for example, a radial force at the grip, we cannot determine without a model how much of that force is: - The golfer actively pulling inward (input)

Centrifugal force from the club’s rotation that the golfer is passively resisting (drift)
Some combination of both

[Figure: In a rotating golf club system, inverse dynamics measures total force at the grip. Without a model, we cannot separate passive forces (centrifugal, gravitational) from active control inputs applied by the golfer.]

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
text:
Limitation 3: The Air Resistance Problem

The Neglected External Force
A factor that is often overlooked in golf swing inverse dynamics is air resistance. While air resistance cannot be significantly manipulated by the golfer, ignoring it can substantially influence our interpretation of the data. Unlike gravity, which is always included in inverse dynamics calculations, air resistance is typically neglected under the assumption that it is small. However, at the high speeds encountered in the golf swing, this assumption may not be justified.


Magnitude of Air Resistance
Research on driver aerodynamics provides insight into the magnitude of air drag forces. Henrikson and Wood measured drag forces on drivers at 100 mph ranging from 6.5 to 9 N (approximately 1.5 to 2 lbs) depending on clubhead design and orientation. A 7 iron at 95 mph likely experiences similar drag forces, as the iron’s less aerodynamic profile may offset the slightly lower speed.
For typical impact conditions: - Clubhead speed: \(\approx\) 95 mph (7 iron)

Estimated drag force: \(\approx\) 2 lbs
Drag acts approximately 1 inch from the end of the club (near the aerodynamic center of the clubhead)

While 2 lbs may seem small compared to the total forces on the club (which can exceed 100 lbs), the key issue is where this force acts and how it affects the moment balance.


Effect on Force and Couple Calculations
When air resistance is neglected, inverse dynamics attributes all the force required to produce the observed acceleration to the golfer’s hands. Let’s examine what happens when we account for air drag using data from Sasho MacKenzie’s user reference frame video.
Consider impact conditions for a 7 iron: - Club length: 37 inches

Grip midpoint location: 3.5 inches from end of grip
COM location: 10 inches from end of club
Reported force at midpoint (no drag): \(F_\alpha = 7.5\) lbs
Reported couple at midpoint (no drag): \(C_\alpha = -18.4\) Nm

Step 1: Calculate Moment of Force Without Drag
Distance from midpoint to COM: \(d_m = 23.5\) inches = 0.597 m
Moment of force about midpoint:
\[
M_{mh} = F_\alpha \cdot d_m = 33.4 \text{ N} \times 0.597 \text{ m} = 19.9 \text{ Nm}
\]
Step 2: Account for Air Drag
Drag force: \(F_{\text{drag}} = 2\) lbs = 8.9 N acting 1 inch from club end (9 inches = 0.229 m from COM)
Moment contribution from drag (negative because it opposes rotation):
\[
M_{\text{drag}} = -8.9 \text{ N} \times 0.229 \text{ m} = -2.0 \text{ Nm}
\]
Step 3: Calculate Revised Force at Hands
If drag provides 2.0 Nm of negative moment, the remaining force at the hands must provide:
\[
M_{\text{hands}} = 19.9 - (-2.0) = 21.9 \text{ Nm}
\]
But wait—this is incorrect. The total moment must remain constant (it’s determined by the observed motion). Instead:
Net force at hands after accounting for drag:
\[
F_{\text{hands}} = 7.5 - 2 = 5.5 \text{ lbs} = 24.5 \text{ N}
\]
Moment from hands force:
\[
M_{\text{hands}} = 24.5 \text{ N} \times 0.597 \text{ m} = 14.6 \text{ Nm}
\]
Total moment (hands + drag):
\[
M_{\text{total}} = 14.6 + (-2.0) = 12.6 \text{ Nm}
\]
This is 7.3 Nm less than the no-drag case! The sum of moments must equal what inverse dynamics calculated, so:
\[
C_{\alpha,\text{drag}} = M_{\text{total}} - M_{mh} = 12.6 - 19.9 = -7.3 \text{ Nm}
\]
Comparison: - Without drag consideration: \(C_\alpha = -18.4\) Nm

With drag consideration: \(C_\alpha = -11.1\) Nm

This represents a **40

[Figure: Effect of accounting for air resistance on force and couple calculations. When drag is neglected, inverse dynamics attributes all forces to the golfer’s hands, leading to substantially different couple values.]


Broader Implications
The air resistance effect demonstrates a third source of ambiguity in inverse dynamics interpretation:

Fundamental Limitation: Neglecting air resistance leads to systematic errors in calculated forces and couples. Because drag acts far from the grip, its moment contribution is substantial despite its relatively modest magnitude. The resulting errors are: - Non-uniform across the swing (speed-dependent)

Most significant near impact (highest speeds)
Spatially biased (affects couples more than net forces)


This has particular relevance for the alpha torque debate. If one researcher includes drag in their model while another neglects it, they will calculate systematically different couple values from identical motion data. The 40



Why Air Resistance Matters for Interpretation
Unlike the spatial ambiguity (which requires knowing force distribution) or the drift-input ambiguity (which requires a full dynamic model), the air resistance problem is:

Systematic: It always acts in a known direction (opposing motion)
Estimable: Magnitude can be approximated from aerodynamic studies
Correctable: Can be included in inverse dynamics with reasonable assumptions
Significant: 40



Key Point: Air resistance should not be neglected in high-speed golf swing analysis, particularly when interpreting couples/torques. Including drag in the inverse dynamics calculation provides more accurate estimates of the forces actually applied by the golfer.

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
section: The Path from Inverse Dynamics to Golfer Effort
text:
The Path from Inverse Dynamics to Golfer Effort

The Triple Indeterminacy
We have now identified three independent sources of ambiguity in inverse dynamics results:

Spatial ambiguity (Section 2): Where are forces applied along the grip?
Drift-input ambiguity (Section 3): What portion of measured forces is passive vs. active?
External force ambiguity (Section 4): How much do neglected external forces (especially air resistance) affect the results?

These ambiguities compound each other. Even perfect knowledge of one aspect leaves the others unresolved.


Required Tools and Information
To successfully interpret inverse dynamics, we need:
[Table]

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
text:
Quantitative Examples

Example 1: Impact Zone Force Interpretation
Consider a typical scenario approaching impact. Motion capture yields the club’s acceleration, and inverse dynamics calculates: - Net force at grip midpoint: \(F_m = 60\) lbs = 267 N (toward target)

Couple at grip midpoint: \(C_m = -4.5\) Nm (negative = counter-rotation)

Assume grip parameters: - Distance from midpoint to COM: \(d_m = 30\) in = 0.762 m

Left hand predominantly at \(d_L = 32\) in = 0.813 m from COM
Right hand predominantly at \(d_R = 28\) in = 0.711 m from COM

Spatial ambiguity analysis:
Equivalent couple at left hand:
\[
\begin{align}
C_L &= M_m \left(1 - \frac{d_L}{d_m}\right) + C_m \\
&= (267 \times 0.762) \left(1 - \frac{0.813}{0.762}\right) + (-4.5) \\
&= 203 \times (-0.067) - 4.5 \\
&= -13.6 - 4.5 = -18.1 \text{ Nm}
\end{align}
\]
Equivalent couple at right hand:
\[
\begin{align}
C_R &= M_m \left(1 - \frac{d_R}{d_m}\right) + C_m \\
&= 203 \times (0.067) - 4.5 \\
&= 13.6 - 4.5 = 9.1 \text{ Nm}
\end{align}
\]

Key Point: The equivalent couple changes sign depending on reference point! At the midpoint, inverse dynamics shows negative couple (counter-rotation). But if force is primarily applied at the right hand, the equivalent couple at that location is positive (pro-rotation).



Example 2: Drift vs. Input Decomposition
Consider mid-downswing with the club rotating at \(\omega = 30\) rad/s. Inverse dynamics measures radial force at grip: \(F_{\text{radial}} = 100\) lbs (inward).
Without a model: We know the club experiences 100 lbs total radial force.
With a model: Suppose the club has: - Mass: \(m_c = 0.5\) lbs

Effective radius from pivot: \(r = 3\) ft

Centrifugal force (drift component):
\[
F_{\text{centrifugal}} = \frac{m_c}{g} \omega^2 r = \frac{0.5}{32.2} \times (30)^2 \times 3 \approx 42 \text{ lbs}
\]
This is drift—it exists whether or not the golfer pulls. The active input component is:
\[
F_{\text{input}} = F_{\text{total}} - F_{\text{drift}} = 100 - 42 = 58 \text{ lbs}
\]
So the golfer actively pulls inward with 58 lbs (what they feel), while 42 lbs of the measured force is passive resistance to centrifugal effects.
[Figure: Decomposition of measured radial force into drift (passive centrifugal) and input (active) components. The drift component grows quadratically with angular velocity. The input component represents what the golfer actively controls and feels.]

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
text:
Implications and Best Practices

For Golf Instruction
When using inverse dynamics data for instruction: - A reported couple may not correspond to twisting sensations the golfer feels

Forces golfers “feel” correspond more closely to input (active control) than to total forces
Passive dynamics (drift) are often substantial but may not be consciously perceived
External forces like air resistance can significantly affect calculated values
Different golfers may achieve similar inverse dynamics outcomes through different strategies



For Biomechanics Research
Methodological recommendations:

Specify reference points: Always state the reference point and acknowledge spatial ambiguity
Report ranges: Consider reporting equivalent couples at multiple reference points
Include all external forces: Don’t neglect air resistance at high speeds
Use models: Separate drift from input whenever possible
Seek direct measurements: Instrumented grips reduce reliance on inverse dynamics alone
Be precise in language: Distinguish between:

“What is happening to the club” (inverse dynamics can tell us)



“What the golfer is doing” (requires additional interpretation)



The Alpha Torque Debate Revisited
The alpha torque debate involves all three ambiguities:

Reference point dependence: Sign of couple changes with assumed force location
Drift-input conflation: Some measured torque arises from passive dynamics
Air resistance: Neglecting drag can cause 40


A productive path forward requires instrumented grips, validated models including drag, analysis at multiple reference points, and recognition that different golfers may use genuinely different strategies.

title: Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics: Understanding the Fundamental Limitations
text:
Conclusion
Inverse dynamics is a valuable tool for analyzing golf swing mechanics. However, interpreting its results requires navigating three fundamental challenges:

Spatial ambiguity: Force-couple pairs are reference point dependent
Drift-input separation: Total forces include both passive and active components
External forces: Neglecting air resistance introduces systematic errors

These are inherent properties of the inverse problem, not shortcomings of the method. The path forward requires:

Building validated biomechanical models
Including all relevant external forces (especially drag)
Using instrumented grips for direct measurement
Specifying reference points clearly
Recognizing that what golfers “feel” is the input component

Understanding these limitations enables more informed use of inverse dynamics in both research and instruction.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
Golf impact presents an apparent paradox. Elite players simultaneously produce very large forces at the hands and clubhead while maintaining remarkably stable clubface orientation during the most violent phase of the swing. Traditional explanations often appeal to vague notions of “firm wrists,” “holding angles,” or “releasing late,” none of which clearly explain how force amplification and stability coexist in a highly redundant, flexible, biological system.
This article proposes a more precise interpretation: near impact, skilled golfers intentionally collapse portions of the constraint Jacobian of the golfer–club system, selectively reducing mobility in destabilizing directions while preserving mobility in force-productive directions.
In mechanical terms, this is not brute stiffness, nor passive locking. It is targeted constraint shaping, achieved through configuration, redundancy, and internal force generation.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
section: 2 2. The Golfer–Club System as a Constrained Mechanism
text:
2 2. The Golfer–Club System as a Constrained Mechanism
Consider the golfer and club as a constrained multibody system with generalized coordinates \(q\). The club is coupled to the hands through bilateral constraints, and the hands themselves are linked through the torso and upper limbs, forming a closed kinematic chain.
Let the constraint equations be written as:
\[
\phi(q) = 0
\]
with constraint Jacobian:
\[
J_c(q) = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial q}
\]
The equations of motion under constraints are:
\[
M(q)\ddot{q} + h(q,\dot{q}) = S^\top \tau + J_c^\top \lambda
\]
where: - \(M(q)\) is the mass matrix, - \(h\) contains Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravity terms, - \(\tau\) are joint torques, - \(\lambda\) are constraint forces enforcing the hand–club coupling.
Crucially, forces transmitted to the club are mediated by \(\lambda\), not directly by joint torques.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
3 3. Constraint-Space Inertia and Force Amplification
The relationship between applied torques and constraint forces depends on the constraint-space inertia:
\[
\Lambda_c = \left(J_c M^{-1} J_c^\top\right)^{-1}
\]
When \(\Lambda_c\) becomes large in a particular direction, small joint torques can generate large constraint forces without requiring large accelerations.
This is the mechanical origin of force amplification near kinematic singularities and poorly conditioned Jacobians in robotics. The same mathematics applies to human movement.
A “collapsed” constraint Jacobian does not imply complete loss of motion. Instead, it implies:

Reduced mobility in selected directions,
Increased force transmission along complementary directions.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
4 4. What “Constraint Collapse” Means in Golf (Biomechanically)
In golf, the goal is not to collapse the entire Jacobian. That would sacrifice control and robustness. Instead, elite golfers exhibit anisotropic collapse:

High mechanical impedance (stiffness/damping) approaching the limit of a kinematic constraint. While not a true geometric singularity (which would imply bone-on-bone locking), the neuromuscular co-contraction creates a ‘virtual constraint’ that mimics a reduction in degrees of freedom in:

Clubface twist about the shaft axis,
Loft and lie perturbations,
Handle motion orthogonal to the intended delivery direction.

Preserved mobility in:

The primary release direction that generates clubhead speed,
The intended swing path curvature.


This selective conditioning allows the club to behave as a stiff tool at impact, while remaining dynamically efficient earlier in the swing.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
5 5. Internal Forces and Redundancy Exploitation
Because the golfer grips the club with two hands separated along the shaft, the system is kinematically redundant. This redundancy allows the generation of internal forces:

Forces that do not change the gross club motion,
But increase normal forces, torsional stiffness, and stability.







Note



These internal forces do not perform work on the club’s center of mass motion (orthogonality), but they modulate the apparent stiffness of the grasp interface.


Mathematically, internal forces lie in the nullspace of the task Jacobian:
\[
\tau = \tau_{\text{task}} + N^\top \tau_{\text{internal}}
\]
where \(N\) projects into the nullspace of the club motion task.
Near impact, skilled golfers exploit this redundancy to: - Increase axial push–pull along the grip, - Generate counter-torques about the shaft axis, - Suppress small perturbations that would otherwise rotate the clubface.
Importantly, these internal forces do not add speed—they add control.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
section: 6 6. Timing: Late Constraint Stiffening, Not Early Locking
text:
6 6. Timing: Late Constraint Stiffening, Not Early Locking
A critical feature of this strategy is timing.
If high constraint stiffness were applied early: - Energy transfer would be reduced, - Sensitivity to timing errors would increase, - Speed generation would suffer.
Instead, constraint collapse occurs late, during the final approach to impact. This corresponds to a stiffness pulse, not a static posture.
In control terms, the golfer increases effective constraint stiffness and damping only when robustness matters most—during collision with the ball.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
section: 7 7. Relationship to Drift and Control (Affine Dynamics View)
text:
7 7. Relationship to Drift and Control (Affine Dynamics View)
From an affine control perspective:
\[
\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u
\]

The drift term \(f(x)\) dominates the high-speed motion of the club,
The control term \(g(x)u\) is primarily used to shape constraints, not drive speed.

Constraint collapse is therefore not about “powering” the club through impact. It is about controlling how drift-generated momentum is delivered.
This distinction explains why elite players can look “passive” near impact while still producing enormous forces.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
8 8. Observable Consequences and Testable Predictions
This framework makes concrete, testable predictions:

Reduced sensitivity of clubface angle to joint perturbations near impact: \[
\delta \theta_{\text{face}} \approx \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial q}\,\delta q \downarrow
\]
Increased internal force proxies (e.g., grip force asymmetry, forearm co-contraction) without increased clubhead acceleration.
Anisotropic operational-space inertia at the clubhead:

High effective mass along face-stability axes,
Lower effective mass along speed-generation axes.


These effects should be observable in high-resolution motion capture, force proxies, or inverse dynamics reconstructions.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
9 9. Implications
Understanding impact stability as intentional constraint Jacobian shaping reframes several long-standing debates in golf science:

“Firm wrists” are not rigid locks, but directional impedance shaping.
Stability does not require eliminating motion, only eliminating the wrong motion.
Power and control are not opposing goals when redundancy and constraints are exploited correctly.

The golfer is not fighting physics at impact—they are leaning into it.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
10 10. Conclusion
Near impact, elite golfers intentionally collapse selected directions of the constraint Jacobian, creating a mechanical environment where:

Large forces are transmitted efficiently,
Destabilizing degrees of freedom are suppressed,
Drift-driven momentum is delivered with precision.

This strategy is neither mystical nor accidental. It is a consequence of redundancy, timing, and constraint-aware control in a highly evolved biological system.
Understanding it requires moving beyond kinematics alone—and taking constraints seriously.

title: Intentional Constraint Collapse at Impact: How Golfers Generate High Force with Stable Club Motion
text:
11 11. Synthesis: The AffineDrift Context
The “Effective Plant” and Drift Invariance This constraint shaping mechanism offers a quasi-static resolution to the “Input-Dependent Boundary Conditions” critique (detailed in Part 3 Limitations). By treating the high-impedance state as a temporary “Effective Plant,” we can analyze the impact dynamics as if they evolved on a restricted manifold, acknowledging that the transition to this state is itself input-driven. While the Affine Control framework assumes a separation of passive drift (\(f(x)\)) and active input (\(g(x)u\)), constraint collapse illustrates how input \(u\) modifies the effective topology of the system. By stiffening the constraint Jacobian \(J_c\), the golfer temporarily alters the manifold on which the drift dynamics evolve, essentially creating a transient “effective plant” without violating the causal independence of the underlying Lagrangian mechanics.






ImportantLimitation: The Stiffness Pulse Paradox



We must strictly qualify this “Effective Plant” argument. The “Stiffness Pulse” described in Section 6 implies a rapid time-variation of the impedance parameters \(\dot{K} \neq 0\) during the counterfactual integration window. This violates the strict Drift Invariance condition (\(\nabla_u f(x) = 0\)) because the drift field parameters are changing in correlation with the input strategy. Consequently, the ZTCF in this regime should be interpreted as a Parametric Counterfactual (“What if torque ceased but the impedance schedule continued?”) rather than a purely passive mechanical baseline.


Steering the Zero-Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) In the context of the ZTCF baseline (Theory Part 2), constraint collapse functions as the “funnel” for passive momentum. The ZTCF describes the massive kinetic potential of the double-pendulum release; the collapsed constraint Jacobian ensures this energy is not dissipated into instability (e.g., face twist) upon impact. The input \(u\) does not push the club through impact; it locks the gates to force the drift \(f(x)\) to exit through the ball.
Null Space as a Control Reserve The “Internal Forces” described here provide the physical mechanism for the “Geometric Rejection of Disturbance” discussed in the Universal Wrist Joint analysis. By occupying the null space of the task Jacobian, the golfer creates a reservoir of stiffness that remains causally distinct from the motion-generating torques, validating the decomposition of torque into “Configuration-driving” and “Shape-holding” components.

11.1 See Also

Theory Part 3: For the formal “Force Taxonomy” distinguishing drift from input.
Theory Part 2: For the definition of the ZTCF and the role of passive momentum.
Wrist Universal Joint: For the specific kinematics of the hand-wrist interface governing these constraints.
Nonlinear Control Insights: For the Lie Bracket interpretation of deceleration as a steering mechanism.

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
For an affine control system, we usually write \[
\dot{x} = f(x) + G(x)u,
\] and think of \(f\) as the drift (what the system does “on its own”) and \(G(x)u\) as the control effect.
For mechanical systems, there is a direct analog at the level of forces, torques, and wrenches:

A natural (or drift) component that arises purely from

inertia,
Coriolis and centrifugal effects,
gravity,
damping/friction,
contact reactions;

An active component generated by muscular (or actuator) input.

The key point:

For a given motion and environment, the total torques and wrenches can be decomposed into a purely natural mechanical contribution plus an active contribution generated by muscles/actuators. This is not a control design issue; it is a mechanical identity.

In this article:

We derive this decomposition in general form.
We specialize it to a planar double pendulum.
We implement the model in Python (ready to be wrapped in Streamlit).

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
For an affine control system, we usually write \[
\dot{x} = f(x) + G(x)u,
\] and think of \(f\) as the drift (what the system does “on its own”) and \(G(x)u\) as the control effect.
For mechanical systems, there is a direct analog at the level of forces, torques, and wrenches:

A natural (or drift) component that arises purely from

inertia,

gravity,

contact reactions;

An active component generated by muscular (or actuator) input.

The key point:

For a given motion and environment, the total torques and wrenches can be decomposed into a purely natural mechanical contribution plus an active contribution generated by muscles/actuators. This is not a control design issue; it is a mechanical identity.

In this article:

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
section: 2. General mechanical system: natural vs active torques
text:
2. General mechanical system: natural vs active torques
Consider an \(n\)-DOF mechanical system with generalized coordinates \(q \in \mathbb{R}^n\), velocities \(\dot{q}\), accelerations \(\ddot{q}\). The standard joint-space dynamics (from Lagrange or Newton–Euler) can be written as
\[
M(q)\,\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\,\dot{q} + g(q) + d(q,\dot{q})
= \tau_{\text{in}} + \tau_{\text{ext}},
\tag{2.1}
\]
where

\(M(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is the inertia matrix,
\(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}\) is the vector of Coriolis and centrifugal terms,
\(g(q)\) is the gravity torque vector,
\(d(q,\dot{q})\) collects dissipative effects (e.g., joint damping, friction),
\(\tau_{\text{in}}\) are internal active torques (e.g., muscles or motors),
\(\tau_{\text{ext}}\) are generalized forces from external wrenches.

Suppose external wrenches \(\lambda\) (contact forces, etc.) act at some contact frames with Jacobian \(J_c(q)\). Then
\[
\tau_{\text{ext}} = J_c(q)^\top \lambda.
\tag{2.2}
\]
Substituting into (2.1),
\[
M(q)\,\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\,\dot{q} + g(q) + d(q,\dot{q})
= \tau_{\text{in}} + J_c(q)^\top \lambda.
\tag{2.3}
\]

2.1 Natural torque field
We define the natural (drift) torque field as the part entirely determined by the motion and environment:
\[
\tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda)
:= M(q)\ddot{q}
+ C(q,\dot{q})\,\dot{q}
+ g(q)
+ d(q,\dot{q})
- J_c(q)^\top \lambda.
\tag{2.4}
\]
Interpretation:

\(\tau_{\text{nat}}\) is what the world contributes:

inertial reaction torques,
velocity-dependent terms,
gravity,
dissipation,
plus minus the external generalized forces (so that the remaining side is “internal”).

It depends only on the trajectory and environment: \((q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda)\).
No reference to “control design” or “desired motion” appears here.

From (2.3) and (2.4), we have the identity
\[
\tau_{\text{in}} = \tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda).
\tag{2.5}
\]
In words: for whatever motion you actually observe or simulate, the internal active torques equal the natural torque field given by the mass matrix, Coriolis, gravity, damping, and external wrenches.


2.2 Parametrizing active torque by inputs
Now suppose the internal active torques are generated by some input vector \(u \in \mathbb{R}^m\):
\[
\tau_{\text{in}} = B(q)\,u,
\tag{2.6}
\]
where \(B(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\) is a configuration-dependent actuation matrix (mapping “muscle channels” or actuators into joint space).
Combining (2.5) and (2.6):
\[
B(q)\,u = \tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda).
\tag{2.7}
\]
This is a purely mechanical identity:

Given the state trajectory and external forces, \(\tau_{\text{nat}}\) is determined.
Given a model of how muscles/actuators generate torque (\(B(q)\)), the input channels \(u\) must satisfy (2.7).

If \(B(q)\) has full column rank, a typical reconstruction of \(u\) is
\[
u = B(q)^{+}\,\tau_{\text{nat}},
\tag{2.8}
\]
where \((\cdot)^{+}\) is a pseudoinverse.

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
3. State-space drift vs active contribution
We can also describe the same decomposition at the state level, in the usual first-order form.
Define the state
\[
x = \begin{bmatrix} q \\ \dot{q} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}.
\]
From (2.3) and (2.6),
\[
M(q)\ddot{q}
= B(q)u + J_c(q)^\top \lambda
  - C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}
  - g(q)
  - d(q,\dot{q}).
\tag{3.1}
\]
Therefore
\[
\ddot{q}
= M(q)^{-1}\,
\big(
  J_c(q)^\top \lambda
  - C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}
  - g(q)
  - d(q,\dot{q})
\big)
+ M(q)^{-1} B(q)\,u.
\tag{3.2}
\]
Thus
\[
\dot{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\dot{q} \\
M(q)^{-1}\big(
  J_c(q)^\top \lambda
  - C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}
  - g(q)
  - d(q,\dot{q})
\big)
\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
M(q)^{-1} B(q)
\end{bmatrix} u.
\tag{3.3}
\]
Define the natural drift field
\[
f_{\text{nat}}(x,\lambda)
:=
\begin{bmatrix}
\dot{q} \\
M(q)^{-1}\big(
  J_c(q)^\top \lambda
  - C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}
  - g(q)
  - d(q,\dot{q})
\big)
\end{bmatrix},
\tag{3.4}
\]
and the input field
\[
G(x) :=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
M(q)^{-1} B(q)
\end{bmatrix}.
\tag{3.5}
\]
Then we have the familiar affine structure:
\[
\dot{x} = f_{\text{nat}}(x,\lambda) + G(x)u.
\tag{3.6}
\]
Here, \(f_{\text{nat}}\) is exactly the evolution the system would have with no active input (\(u = 0\)), subject to gravity, contact, damping, and current velocities.

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
section: 4. Wrench-level decomposition: natural vs active wrench
text:
4. Wrench-level decomposition: natural vs active wrench
Consider an end-effector (e.g., a point on the club) with a spatial Jacobian \(J(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times n}\) that maps joint velocities to twist:
\[
v = J(q)\,\dot{q}, \qquad v \in \mathbb{R}^6.
\]
The spatial wrench \(w \in \mathbb{R}^6\) (force and moment) maps to joint space as
\[
\tau_{\text{joint}} \approx J(q)^\top\,w + \tau_{\text{int}},
\tag{4.1}
\]
where \(\tau_{\text{int}}\) collects internal constraint forces that do not appear as net wrench at that end-effector. If we ignore or separately model those internal contributions, we approximate
\[
\tau_{\text{joint}} \approx J(q)^\top w.
\tag{4.2}
\]
Given joint torques \(\tau\), we can approximate the corresponding wrench by a pseudoinverse:
\[
w \approx \big(J(q)^\top\big)^{+}\,\tau.
\tag{4.3}
\]

4.1 Natural wrench
Using the natural torque field \(\tau_{\text{nat}}\), define the natural wrench at the end-effector:
\[
w_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda)
:= \big(J(q)^\top\big)^{+}
   \,\tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda).
\tag{4.4}
\]
This is the wrench associated with inertia, gravity, velocity-dependent terms, dissipation, and contacts, mapped to the end-effector.


4.2 Active wrench
From (2.6), the active torque is \(B(q)u\). The associated active wrench is
\[
w_{\text{act}}(q,u)
:= \big(J(q)^\top\big)^{+} B(q)\,u.
\tag{4.5}
\]
Define
\[
W(q) := \big(J(q)^\top\big)^{+} B(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{6 \times m},
\tag{4.6}
\]
so that
\[
w_{\text{act}}(q,u) = W(q)\,u.
\tag{4.7}
\]
Each column of \(W(q)\) is the wrench direction generated by unit activation of one input channel.


4.3 Total wrench decomposition
The total wrench splits as
\[
w(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda,u)
=
w_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q},\lambda)
+
w_{\text{act}}(q,u),
\tag{4.8}
\]
i.e.
\[
w = w_{\text{nat}} + W(q)\,u.
\tag{4.9}
\]
This is the wrench-level analog of the usual affine decomposition: natural mechanics vs active input.

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
5. Planar double pendulum example
We now specialize the above to a planar double pendulum (2-link planar manipulator). This gives a concrete model you can drive from Python and plug into Streamlit.

5.1 Configuration and parameters
Let

\(q = \begin{bmatrix} q_1 \\ q_2 \end{bmatrix}\) where

\(q_1\) = angle of link 1 from vertical (or from some fixed axis),
\(q_2\) = relative angle of link 2 from link 1.

Link lengths: \(l_1, l_2\).
Center-of-mass distances along each link: \(c_1, c_2\).
Masses: \(m_1, m_2\).
Inertia about COM (out of plane): \(I_1, I_2\).
Gravity: \(g > 0\).

We assume no explicit damping (for simplicity), i.e. \(d(q,\dot{q}) = 0\), and no external contacts (\(J_c^\top\lambda = 0\)).
Then the equations of motion take the canonical form
\[
M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\,\dot{q} + g(q) = \tau_{\text{in}},
\tag{5.1}
\]
with \(\tau_{\text{in}} = \begin{bmatrix} \tau_1 \\ \tau_2 \end{bmatrix}\) the joint torques.


5.2 Inertia matrix \(M(q)\)
A standard planar 2-link manipulator model gives:
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_{11}(q) &= I_1 + I_2
          + m_1 c_1^2
          + m_2 \big( l_1^2 + c_2^2 + 2 l_1 c_2 \cos q_2 \big), \\
M_{12}(q) &= I_2 + m_2\big( c_2^2 + l_1 c_2 \cos q_2 \big), \\
M_{21}(q) &= M_{12}(q), \\
M_{22}(q) &= I_2 + m_2 c_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.2}
\]
So
\[
M(q) =
\begin{bmatrix}
M_{11}(q) & M_{12}(q) \\
M_{21}(q) & M_{22}(q)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]


5.3 Coriolis/centrifugal terms \(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}\)
There are various equivalent parameterizations. A commonly used one defines
\[
h(q) = - m_2 l_1 c_2 \sin q_2.
\tag{5.3}
\]
Then the product \(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}\) can be written as
\[
C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} =
\begin{bmatrix}
h(q)\dot{q}_2(2\dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2) \\
- h(q)\dot{q}_1^2
\end{bmatrix}.
\tag{5.4}
\]
You can think of this as \(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}\) without ever writing out \(C\) explicitly as a matrix.


5.4 Gravity term \(g(q)\)
Assuming angles are measured from the downward vertical for simplicity, the gravity torques are
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_1(q) &= (m_1 c_1 + m_2 l_1)\,g\,\sin q_1
       + m_2 c_2 g \sin(q_1 + q_2), \\
g_2(q) &= m_2 c_2 g \sin(q_1 + q_2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.5}
\]
So
\[
g(q) = \begin{bmatrix} g_1(q) \\ g_2(q) \end{bmatrix}.
\]


5.5 Natural torques and active input
With no external contacts and no explicit damping, the natural torque field reduces to
\[
\tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q})
= M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + g(q).
\tag{5.6}
\]
For a fully actuated system with inputs directly equal to torques, we can set \(B(q) = I_2\) (the \(2\times 2\) identity), so that
\[
\tau_{\text{in}} = u.
\tag{5.7}
\]
The mechanical identity (2.7) becomes
\[
u = \tau_{\text{nat}}(q,\dot{q},\ddot{q}).
\tag{5.8}
\]
In a golf-swing context or in human biomechanics, you might replace \(B(q)\) by a more structured mapping from muscle activations to joint torques; the decomposition still holds.

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
6. Energy Transfer Decomposition
A critical aspect of the drift–control analysis is understanding power flow: how energy moves between segments and how much of that transfer is due to “natural” dynamics versus “active” input.
For a distal segment (e.g., the club, link 2), the total energy \(E_2\) changes due to work done by the joint constraint force \(\vec{F}_{21}\) and the joint torque \(\tau_{21}\).
\[
\dot{E}_2 = \vec{F}_{21} \cdot \vec{v}_{\text{joint}} + \tau_{21} \, \omega_2.
\]
We calculate the joint constraint force \(\vec{F}_{21}\) from Newton’s law applied to the COM of link 2:
\[
\vec{F}_{21} = m_2 (\vec{a}_{c2} - \vec{g}).
\]
Using the affine decomposition of acceleration from (3.2), \[
\ddot{q} = \ddot{q}_{\text{nat}} + M(q)^{-1} B(q) u,
\] the linear acceleration of the COM \(\vec{a}_{c2}\) decomposes as:
\[
\vec{a}_{c2}
= J_{c2} \ddot{q} + \dot{J}_{c2} \dot{q}
= \underbrace{(J_{c2} \ddot{q}_{\text{nat}} + \dot{J}_{c2} \dot{q})}_{\text{natural acceleration } \vec{a}_{\text{nat}}}
  + \underbrace{(J_{c2} M(q)^{-1} B(q) u)}_{\text{active acceleration } \vec{a}_{\text{act}}}.
\]
Thus, the constraint force splits into natural and active components:
\[
\vec{F}_{\text{nat}} = m_2 (\vec{a}_{\text{nat}} - \vec{g}), \qquad
\vec{F}_{\text{act}} = m_2 \vec{a}_{\text{act}}.
\]
Depending on the actuator model, the joint torque \(\tau_{21}\) also splits (e.g., into passive spring/damper \(\tau_{\text{nat}}\) and active motor \(\tau_{\text{act}}\)). For a purely torque-driven joint, \(\tau_{21} = \tau_{\text{act}} = u_2\).
The Power Transfer then decomposes into:

Natural Power Transfer: Energy moved into the link by passive dynamics (e.g., the arm “pulling” on the club due to centripetal acceleration). \[
P_{\text{nat}} = \vec{F}_{\text{nat}} \cdot \vec{v}_{\text{joint}} + \tau_{\text{nat}} \omega_2.
\]
Active Power Transfer: Energy moved into the link by the instantaneous action of the control inputs. \[
P_{\text{act}} = \vec{F}_{\text{act}} \cdot \vec{v}_{\text{joint}} + \tau_{\text{act}} \omega_2.
\]

This decomposition allows us to answer: “Is the club gaining energy because I am pulling on it (passive/geometric transfer) or because I am twisting it (active transfer)?”

title: Natural vs Active Forces and Torques in Affine Mechanical Systems
text:
Theoretical Synthesis

Affine Realization of the Drift Wrench
The decomposition of the total wrench \(w\) into \(w_{\text{nat}}\) and \(w_{\text{act}}\) provides the explicit mechanical realization of the abstract affine control form \(\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u\). Specifically, \(w_{\text{nat}}\) corresponds to the “Drift Wrench” generated by the vector field \(f(x)\), encapsulating all inertial, gravitational, and centripetal history of the system. In contrast, \(w_{\text{act}}\) represents the instantaneous “Control Authority” \(g(x)u\). This separation is critical for verifying the Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF): setting \(u=0\) (and thus \(w_{\text{act}}=0\)) isolates the \(w_{\text{nat}}\) component, proving that the clubhead’s acceleration in the ZTCF is not zero, but rather driven entirely by the “Natural Wrench” of the kinematic chain.


Resolving Teleological Blindness
The energy transfer decomposition in Section 6 resolves the “Teleological Blindness” often found in kinetic analyses. By distinguishing \(P_{\text{nat}}\) from \(P_{\text{act}}\), we can rigorously attribute clubhead speed generation to either “Geometric Work” (energy transfer via constraint forces \(\vec{F}_{\text{nat}}\), e.g., the centripetal pull of the arm) or “Active Work” (energy input via joint torques \(\tau_{\text{act}}\)). This framework exposes the Drift Dominance in the late downswing, where \(P_{\text{nat}} \gg P_{\text{act}}\), confirming that the golfer’s primary role is to establish the geometric conditions (the “Effective Plant”) that maximize passive energy transfer, rather than to actively push the club.


Implicit Assumption: The Stiff Shaft Limit
It is essential to note that this derivation assumes a Rigid Body model for all links. Consequently, the “Active Wrench” \(w_{\text{act}}\) is assumed to transmit instantaneously from the hands to the clubhead. This omits the elastic potential energy storage and release dynamics characteristic of a flexible shaft (the Stretch-Shortening Cycle). In a flexible model, the active input \(u\) would first do work on the shaft stiffness (\(V_{elastic}\)), introducing a phase delay before appearing as kinetic energy at the clubhead. Thus, this rigid-body decomposition represents the “Stiff Shaft Limit” of the true dynamics.


Suggested Cross-References

Theory Part 3 (Force Taxonomy): For the classification of \(f(x)\) components.
The Static Force-Mobility Fallacy: For why examining static force transmission (\(J^T\)) is insufficient without accounting for \(\tau_{nat}\).
Simscape Implementation: For the inclusion of flexible bodies which extends this rigid derivation.

title: “Secondary Axis Stability in Golf Clubs: From Bizarre Physics to Better Putters” format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: false 1. Why “secondary axis stability” matters
We like to pretend the club moves around a nice clean axis:
driver: around your tilted spine
putter: around a mostly vertical axis through your shoulders
Reality is messier. The club changes shape during the swing (shaft bends, droops, lags), the hands don’t rotate perfectly about one fixed axis, and the clubhead’s mass isn’t arranged in a way that’s friendly to stable rotation.
That’s where secondary axis stability comes in:
How stable is the club’s rotation when the actual axis of motion is not one of its “nice” principal axes?
To get there, we’re going to lean on a classic rigid body phenomenon: the intermediate axis theorem (aka tennis racket theorem).

The video: “Bizarre Behavior of Rotating Bodies”

Let’s anchor the discussion on this video:
[ 
]{.quarto-shortcode__ data-is-shortcode=“1” data-raw=“{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/1VPfZ_XzisU

}}“}

This is the well-known “bizarre behavior of rotating bodies” demonstration: flip a rigid object in the air and it behaves fine about two axes… and goes completely weird about the third.
What’s happening is:
Any rigid body has three principal moments of inertia
I1≤I2≤I3 I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
, with associated orthogonal axes.
Rotation about the axes with smallest ( I1 I 1 ​
) or largest ( I3 I 3 ​
) moment is stable.
Rotation about the intermediate axis ( I2 I 2 ​
) is unstable: tiny perturbations grow into big flips.
In free flight, that instability shows up as the famous end-over-end flip. In a golf club:
The club isn’t in free flight (the hands are applying torque),
but the same structure of the equations shows up as sensitive, hard-to-control rotations when the stroke tries to use a “bad” effective axis.
That sensitivity is exactly what you feel as:
inconsistent face closure,
the head “wobbling” off-plane,
or the putter feeling fine on some strokes and alien on others.

The golf club as a changing rigid body 3.1 Principal axes of a club

For a putter head, you can roughly define:
x x-axis: pointing from face toward the back of the head
y y-axis: heel–toe direction
z z-axis: vertical
Ignoring the shaft for a moment, the head has three principal moments:
Ix I x ​
— about the face-back axis
Iy I y ​
— about the heel–toe axis
Iz I z ​
— about the vertical axis (this is the usual forgiveness MOI: resistance to twisting on off-center hits). one-putts.com +2 MDPI +2
Modern mallets push weight out to heel and toe and rearward to maximize Iz I z ​
. Typical numbers:
“Normal” putters: ~3500–6000 g·cm²
High-MOI mallets: ~6000–9000 g·cm² one-putts.com +1
That’s great for impact forgiveness, but says exactly nothing about how stable the head is when the swing axis itself is bouncing around.
3.2 Why the axis isn’t stable
In a real swing, the effective rotation axis of the clubhead is:
set by your body motion (spine tilt, secondary axis tilt, etc.), GolfWRX +2 Rotaryswing.com +2
altered by shaft bend and droop,
shifted by the fact the shaft attaches near the heel, not through the CG, Cal Poly Content +1
and influenced by how your hands “steer” the club (especially in putting).
So the axis the club actually rotates about is some ugly combination of:
your body’s rotation axis,
the shaft axis,
and whatever torque pattern your hands are applying.
That axis usually doesn’t line up with any principal axis of the head. And as the club flexes and deforms, the inertia tensor changes slightly; the principal axes move in relation to the shaft.
This is the recipe for secondary axis drama:
When the effective rotation axis drifts through the neighborhood of the intermediate principal axis, the dynamics get very sensitive.
The torque required at the hands to keep the club “behaving” can spike or change sign faster than your brain can compensate.
You won’t see a full tennis-racket flip because your hands are clamped on the thing, but you will see:
erratic closure rates,
“mysterious” pulls and pushes with what felt like the same stroke,
and a putter that feels livelier or deader depending on tiny differences in path or lie.

Secondary axis stability: a working definition

For our purposes, define secondary axis stability as:
The degree to which the club’s rotation is predictable and self-consistent when the actual swing axis is not one of the primary principal axes.
More formally:
Let I1≤I2≤I3 I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
be principal moments.
Let ω ω be the angular velocity of the clubhead.
If ω ω is aligned with the axis of I1 I 1 ​
or I3 I 3 ​
, rotation is naturally stable.
If ω ω lies near the intermediate axis ( I2 I 2 ​
), small perturbations in torque produce disproportionately large changes in ω ω and in the orientation of the head.
We don’t need full-blown rigid-body math here; the takeaway is:
The more your rotation axis is forced to lie in a region where the inertia tensor is “unfriendly”,
the more you’ll need fine, time-varying hand torques to keep the face stable.
A club with good secondary axis stability does two things:
It makes it hard for your effective rotation axis to wander into the “bad” intermediate regime.
When you do wander, it doesn’t punish you with violent sensitivity.

How putters are currently designed (and what they’re missing) 5.1 High-MOI, perimeter weighting

Modern mallets mostly chase maximum Iz I z ​
(vertical MOI) for impact forgiveness:
Rear and toe/heel weights,
Hollow bodies with mass pushed to the edges,
Some even approach driver-like constraints in spirit (though putters don’t share the USGA driver limit of 5900 g·cm²). Cal Poly Content +1
For off-center hits, this works: a high Iz I z ​
reduces face twist and speed loss. Argolf USA +1
But from a secondary axis perspective:
Perimeter weighting tends to make the inertia ellipsoid very “flat” in certain directions,
which can make the intermediate-axis region sharply defined and more sensitive if the swing axis passes through it.
5.2 Zero-torque and lie-angle-balanced putters
Some modern “zero-torque” or lie-angle-balanced putters attack a related issue:
They aim to align the center of mass with the shaft axis, so the torque about the shaft during the stroke is minimized. tutelman.com +2 MDPI +2
These designs greatly reduce the torque the golfer must apply to keep the face square during the stroke. That’s good.
But they still typically use some form of perimeter weighting, and they don’t explicitly target the stability of rotation when:
lie angle changes a bit,
the stroke goes slightly off-plane, or
the head flexes and the principal axes shift.
In other words: they reduce one source of “fight” (shaft torque) but don’t fully address how the head behaves when the effective rotation axis itself is wandering through secondary-axis territory.

Concept: a “secondary-axis-stable” mallet

Let’s build the concept you proposed:
A mallet putter with mass oriented on its central axis, heaviest in-plane, with light sections on the outer axis.
6.1 Geometry idea
Take a standard mallet envelope:
Heel–toe span w≈100 mm w≈100 mm
Face–back depth d≈40 mm d≈40 mm
Thickness t≈20 mm t≈20 mm
Now compare two designs with the same total mass and outer dimensions:
Perimeter design (typical high-MOI mallet)
Most mass concentrated in heel and toe wings.
Central section relatively hollow/light.
Central-axis design (your concept)
A dense “spine” along the central axis (aligned with the intended stroke plane).
Outer heel and toe regions made significantly lighter.
Optionally align the spine with the shaft insertion and swing plane, not just geometric center.
Intuitively:
Design 1 maximizes Iz I z ​
(about vertical) for forgiveness.
Design 2 reduces Iz I z ​
but brings the principal axes into closer alignment with the shaft/swing plane and makes them less sensitive to shaft flex and small lie-angle changes.

Quantifying the tradeoff: stability vs MOI

Let’s be honest: a precise calculation needs a full 3D CAD model, real material densities, and a dynamic model of the shaft + hands. I don’t have that luxury here, so I’ll show a toy but honest estimate to give you the right scale.
7.1 A simple numerical experiment
Model both heads as a grid of point masses within the same rectangular envelope:
Same overall mass and dimensions,
Only the distribution of density differs.
Assumptions:
Perimeter mallet: Outer ~60% of the heel–toe span is twice as dense as the inner region.
Central-axis mallet: A central bar (say ±15% of heel–toe span) is twice as dense, and the outer wings are made very light (e.g., 1/2 density of the center).
If you compute the inertia tensor about the center of mass and extract the principal moments (I1≤I2≤I3) (I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
), you get something qualitatively like:
Perimeter design (normalized units):
I1≈0.00023 I 1 ​
≈0.00023
I2≈0.00123 I 2 ​
≈0.00123
I3≈0.00133 I 3 ​
≈0.00133
Central-axis design (same mass & envelope):
I1≈0.00023 I 1 ​
≈0.00023
I2≈0.00062 I 2 ​
≈0.00062
I3≈0.00072 I 3 ​
≈0.00072
Interpretation:
The smallest moment I1 I 1 ​
(about the “long” axis) is essentially unchanged — both designs have the same basic footprint.
The largest moment I3 I 3 ​
(which you can loosely associate with vertical-axis MOI in this toy model) drops from ~0.00133 to ~0.00072.
That’s roughly:
I3,centralI3,perimeter≈0.000720.00133≈0.54 I 3,perimeter ​
I 3,central ​
​
≈ 0.00133 0.00072 ​
≈0.54
In other words:
A strong shift from perimeter weighting to central-axis weighting can cut vertical-axis MOI by about 45–50% for the same mass and size.
You can dial this up or down with less extreme weighting, but the direction of the tradeoff is clear:
More central-axis stability → less Iz I z ​
forgiveness.
7.2 Where the stability gain comes from
So why would you ever sacrifice that much MOI? Because you’re trading:
Static forgiveness at impact vs
Dynamic stability of the stroke about off-nominal axes.
Three key effects:
Axis alignment
With mass along a central spine that’s co-linear with the shaft axis and swing plane, the principal axes are more likely to stay aligned with that plane even as the shaft bends.
That means your effective rotation axis is more often close to a stable principal axis (either the min or max I I), and less likely to pass through the intermediate-axis “doom zone”.
Reduced torque variability
The torque your hands must supply to keep the face square is τ=Ieff⋅ω˙+(gyroscopic terms) τ=I eff ​
⋅ ω ˙ +(gyroscopic terms).
If the inertia tensor is more “friendly” relative to the actual stroke axis, then small path deviations or lie-angle changes cause smaller swings in effective inertia and required torque.
Practically: the putter feels like it wants to stay on its path and keep its face angle, instead of needing micro-adjustments.
Smoother behavior under shaft deflection
A perimeter mallet can have principal axes that move a lot when the shaft is bent or the lie angle changes by a few degrees.
A central-axis design tends to make the inertia tensor more axisymmetric with respect to the shaft/swing plane, so those changes have less impact on the rotational dynamics.
You’re effectively saying: “I’m willing to give up some help on bad strikes to get a stroke that’s inherently easier to keep on-plane and square.”
7.3 A rough “stability vs MOI” summary
Using the toy model as a guide (not gospel), you can imagine a family of designs:
Design type Qualitative vertical-axis MOI Qualitative secondary-axis stability Extreme perimeter mallet 100% (baseline) Poor–moderate (sensitive) Modern high-MOI zero-torque mallet 80–100% Moderate (better torque balance) Hybrid perimeter/central spine 60–80% Good Strong central-axis bias (your idea) 50–70% Very good
Those ranges are indicative, not measured. The main point is:
You probably don’t want to go all the way to a 50% MOI design for most golfers;
but a moderate central-axis bias could move you into a sweet spot where:
you lose maybe 20–30% of vertical MOI vs a full perimeter sledgehammer,
and gain a noticeable bump in how “self-stable” the stroke feels about the real, messy swing axis.

Full swing: changing shape, changing axes

Everything above is for a putter, where things are relatively tame. In a full swing, the club is:
bending, drooping, and unbending,
experiencing rapidly changing angular velocity about multiple axes,
and the shaft axis and clubhead principal axes can get badly misaligned at high speed.
In that regime, the intermediate-axis behavior from the video is lurking under the surface:
As the club’s effective inertia tensor changes during the downswing,
the “preferred” stable axes move,
and your actual angular velocity vector can drift closer to, or away from, the intermediate-axis region.
Your hands do an enormous amount of work unconsciously to keep the club behaving. That’s one reason why elite swings look effortless but are absolutely not simple mechanically.
A club designed with secondary axis stability in mind would try to:
Keep the club’s principal axes as “friendly” as possible to the actual path and shaft deflections used in the swing,
so that the club wants to move in the way your body is trying to move it, instead of constantly demanding corrections.
That’s a much harder design problem than “make Iz I z ​
big,” but the physics is the same.

Practical implications for a secondary-axis-stable mallet

If you actually built the putter we just described, here’s what you’d expect:
Pros
Stroke feels more “rail-like”: once you set it in motion, it wants to keep rotating in the same plane.
Less sensitivity to small changes in lie angle or shaft lean during the stroke.
Reduced “wobble” when the hands get a bit out of sync; the putter head behaves more like a single solid axis system.
Potentially simpler, more repeatable face-angle control for players who struggle with face rotation.
Cons
Less built-in forgiveness on mishits — especially for heel–toe strikes.
Marketing nightmare: MOI numbers would look worse on the spec sheet, even if the dynamic stability is better.
Tuning is player-specific: the “right” amount of central weighting depends on stroke style (straight-back-straight-through vs strong arc), lie angle, and shaft insertion geometry.
Who might benefit most?
Players who already strike the ball consistently near the sweet spot,
but fight face control and path consistency under pressure.
Better players who can tolerate a small drop in static forgiveness in exchange for a stroke that feels mechanically “locked in”.

Where this idea fits in the current landscape

The industry has already moved:
From “feel” blades → high-MOI mallets for forgiveness,
Into “zero-torque” and lie-angle-balanced designs that reduce shaft torque and face twist. tutelman.com +2 MDPI +2
The next logical step is exactly what you’re describing:
Putters designed not just for MOI and torque balance, but for stability with respect to the real, messy, changing swing axis — i.e., true secondary axis stability.
That means optimizing:
the full 3D inertia tensor of the head + shaft,
across a range of realistic shaft deflections and lie angles,
to keep the effective stroke axis in a dynamically stable region and to minimize torque variability at the hands.
It’s a more subtle, physics-heavy design space… which is probably why you don’t see it on marketing posters yet.

Summary (for your readers)

The YouTube video on bizarre rotating bodies shows that rotation is only naturally stable about the smallest and largest principal axes. The middle one is an unstable troublemaker.
Golf clubs, especially in motion, don’t rotate about a neat, fixed axis. Shaft flex, body motion, and off-center attachment mean the actual rotation axis wanders, sometimes into that unstable intermediate territory.
Most current putter design focuses on maximizing vertical MOI for impact forgiveness and, more recently, reducing shaft torque (zero-torque, lie-angle balanced). Those are good things but don’t fully address secondary axis stability.
A mallet with mass concentrated along a central spine aligned with the swing plane and shaft can reduce sensitivity to small changes in lie angle and shaft deflection — improving secondary axis stability.
A strong shift from perimeter to central-axis weighting can easily cut vertical-axis MOI by ~40–50% for the same mass and footprint in simple models. That’s a real tradeoff: you’re swapping some impact forgiveness for a stroke that behaves more predictably in 3D.
The smart play is probably not an extreme design, but a hybrid: enough perimeter mass to maintain respectable MOI, plus a robust central spine to tame the secondary axis chaos.
In short: we’ve spent decades making putters that forgive bad impact; the next frontier is making putters that forgive the messy way humans actually move.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
This document outlines practical applications of the control-affine decomposition used in modern multibody golf swing analysis. The decomposition
\[
F_{\text{total}} = F_{\mathrm{drift}} + F_{\mathrm{input}}
\]
is directly actionable for simulation, interpretation of measured forces, model personalization, and advanced data-driven modeling. The material here complements Sections 1–7 by linking theory to practical biomechanics contexts, including the insights developed in prior work on momentum-driven interaction forces.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Counterfactual Analysis (ZTCF)
The Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) isolates passive mechanical effects by evolving the system under
\[
u(t) \equiv 0.
\]
The resulting drift wrench reflects inertial, gravitational, Coriolis, centrifugal, and elastic shaft forces. This is essential for interpreting measured hand–club interaction forces and determining how much of the measured signal arises from momentum transfer rather than active muscular effort.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Estimating Active Effort
Given measured or simulated total force \(F_{\text{total}}\), and drift force \(F_{\mathrm{drift}}\) from ZTCF-based computation, input forces are obtained via
\[
F_{\mathrm{input}} = F_{\text{total}} - F_{\mathrm{drift}}.
\]
This supports reconstruction of active joint torques, improved inverse dynamics, and isolation of the golfer’s actual contribution to club acceleration.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Shaft Mechanics
Shaft deformation contributes only to drift and not to the input mapping. Shaft-related forces should therefore not be interpreted as direct indicators of muscular effort. Changes in stiffness or material properties primarily influence the drift term.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Simulation and Validation
The affine formulation supports: - torque estimation through forward-dynamics matching,

counterfactual mechanical tests,
player-specific simulations based on geometry and inertial parameters.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Data Interpretation
The decomposition provides a rigorous basis for interpreting measured forces, enabling one to classify contributions into passive, active, and constraint-filtered components. This mitigates common misinterpretations where passive effects are inaccurately attributed to active torques.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Machine Learning Applications
ML models can be trained on drift-free input data, improving sample efficiency and interpretability. Drift can also be modeled directly to accelerate simulation, while input torques can be learned as low-dimensional latent representations.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Summary
The control-affine decomposition provides actionable guidance for simulation, measurement interpretation, torque reconstruction, shaft mechanics, and ML-based modeling. The separation of drift and input forces yields a rigorous framework for analyzing and understanding the golf swing.

            At its heart, this website is an attempt to build a website I would like to read. I am an avid golf researcher with an interest in robotics and the mechanics of linked systems. After scouring the web for resources I finally came to the realization that I could just build the website I was looking for with the articles and resources that I was trying to track down.
          
          
          
            Rather than trying to organize my notes offline across multiple devices and formats, why not collect them together in a unified place where others who are also interested can find value in them. To achieve this goal, I have leaned heavily on the assistance of AI models in developing and troubleshooting code and building the website.
          
          
          
            Rather than curate the website myself, I have outlined articles and topics I would like to build or resources that I would like to see and then fed them to AI and importantly - iterated to improve quality. While much of AI-generated golf content can end up as correlational gibberish, there can be significant value when you know how to use it right.
          
          
          
            Rather than asking it for answers, ask it to provide mathematical expressions that can be validated. Ask it to write code that can be reviewed. Ask it to track down sources and links for further information. Every time an article is posted, it is then reviewed by automated bots overnight and feedback is given in the morning. It has been a fun process setting up guardrails to help AI give the most value.
          
          
          
            The agents reviewing the site have different personas. There are editors attempting to improve the fluidity and prose. There is a curator coming up with new topics or avenues to explore. There is a librarian at work in the background curating a cross-linked bibliography of all of the sources that are available. There are mathematicians and mechanics scouring the equations and validating and debugging them.
          
          
          
            Importantly, there are also critics. My goal here is not to hide weakness, but identify it and explore it. The edge cases and shortcomings of a given paradigm often hold extreme value. There is an agent to defend and shore up any technical shortcomings identified by the critics.
          
          
          
            By no means is the website intended to be exhaustive or comprehensive. It is just a place to store resources for myself and construct a technical argument towards the understanding of the viewpoint of the golf swing that I have developed through my years of study. This argument and the site are not complete, nor will they ever be. They will evolve and adapt when new information is identified.
          
          
          
            If this information is of interest to you, feel free to use and share however you choose. I don't care too much about citations personally, but if the information comes from other authors whose work I have linked here, please give credit where credit is due.
          
          
          
            Researching the golf swing is an often fruitless endeavor where you will encounter more than your fair share of critics. An atta boy or tip of the cap to those providing research into the topics we are all mutually interested in is in order when you find something to help you on your way.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text: The golf swing is a high-speed, full-body motion executed by a mechanically complex, constrained multibody system. Conventional inverse dynamics can estimate generalized joint torques and hand forces from motion capture and external force measurements, but it cannot distinguish how much of those forces arise from the golfer’s active muscular effort versus passive mechanical dynamics such as inertia, gravity, and shaft deformation. This paper develops a strictly theoretical framework that models the golfer–club–shaft system as a nonlinear control-affine mechanical system and uses that structure to decompose forces into drift (passive) and input (torque-driven) components. We define the Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) and Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) as mathematical tools for isolating passive dynamics and torque effectiveness, and we derive a force taxonomy that classifies measured forces by their causal origin within the model. Applications and empirical validation will be presented in subsequent simulation and experimental papers.
